title: Hive 7 — honeybee colony: sunken brood cappings and a foul smell
presentation: A twelve-hive apiary. Hive 7 has a dwindling adult population, patchy brood, sunken and perforated cappings, and a distinctly foul smell on opening. Two neighbouring hives were combined with it last month.

stages.title: Inspect the colony
stages.briefing: Brood pattern patchy with a pepperpot appearance. Cappings sunken, darkened and perforated. Affected larvae in the cells are coffee-brown and slumped. Strong foul odour on opening. Adult population declining, queen present and laying. Hive records: frames and hive tool shared between hives without disinfection; two colonies combined into hive 7 last month; no treatment history for brood disease.
stages.prompt: Which findings point to a brood bacterial disease?

options.label: Sunken, perforated cappings over a pepperpot brood pattern
options.detail: Larvae dying after capping

options.label: Coffee-brown slumped larvae in the cells
options.detail: Colour and position typical of American foulbrood

options.label: Foul odour on opening the hive
options.detail: The smell the disease is named for

options.label: Shared frames and hive tool between colonies
options.detail: The transmission route — management, not a clinical sign

options.label: Queen present and laying
options.detail: Rules out a queen failure, but does not identify the disease

stages.explanation: Larvae dying after capping, with sunken perforated cappings and a foul smell, is American foulbrood; larvae dying before capping in twisted positions would be European foulbrood. Getting this distinction right matters more here than in almost any other case in the library, because one of them is notifiable and ends with the colony destroyed.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: You are at the apiary with a matchstick, a lateral flow kit and the ability to submit samples to the national bee laboratory.

options.label: Ropiness (matchstick) test on an affected larva
options.detail: A field test that strongly suggests American foulbrood

options.label: Lateral flow device for Paenibacillus larvae
options.detail: Rapid presumptive confirmation on site

options.label: Submit brood comb to the national reference laboratory for culture and confirmation
options.detail: Statutory confirmation, and it distinguishes the foulbroods

options.label: Inspect and sample all remaining hives in the apiary
options.detail: Defines the extent before anything is moved

options.label: Microscopy of larval smears for spores
options.detail: Spore morphology supports the diagnosis

options.label: Varroa mite count as the primary investigation
options.detail: Essential routine monitoring, but it does not explain foul-smelling capped brood

options.label: Nosema spore count as the diagnostic test
options.detail: An adult bee disease, not a brood disease

stages.explanation: The matchstick test costs nothing and points the way in seconds, but the diagnosis that carries legal consequences has to be confirmed by the reference laboratory. Inspecting the whole apiary before equipment moves again is part of the diagnostic work, because spores travel on frames and tools and the combination last month may already have spread it.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Matchstick test: larval remains draw out in a fine thread 3 cm long (ropy). Lateral flow for Paenibacillus larvae: strong positive. Reference laboratory: Paenibacillus larvae confirmed by culture; Melissococcus plutonius not detected. Larval smears: numerous spore-forming rods. Apiary inspection: hive 9 has two cells with sunken cappings and a weak positive lateral flow; the other ten hives are clear. Varroa count low. Nosema not detected.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: American foulbrood confirmed in hive 7
options.detail: Ropy larvae with Paenibacillus larvae cultured

options.label: Hive 9 is affected early and must be treated as infected
options.detail: Sunken cappings with a weak positive test

options.label: European foulbrood is excluded
options.detail: Melissococcus plutonius not detected

options.label: Shared equipment plausibly spread spores between hives
options.detail: Frames and tools moved without disinfection, plus a colony combination

options.label: Varroa infestation is the primary problem
options.detail: Counts are low and it does not cause ropy capped brood

options.label: Nosema explains the population decline
options.detail: Not detected, and it is a disease of adults

stages.explanation: Ropiness plus a cultured organism is the confirmation, and the distinction from European foulbrood is what determines the legal response. Finding hive 9 early is the most valuable outcome of the visit — it is the difference between losing two colonies and losing the apiary. Excluding varroa and nosema stops a beekeeper treating the wrong disease while spores spread.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Ropy larval remains, strong positive lateral flow, Paenibacillus larvae confirmed on culture, Melissococcus plutonius not detected, hive 9 early-positive, shared equipment between hives.

options.label: American foulbrood (Paenibacillus larvae) in hives 7 and 9, spread by shared equipment
options.detail: Confirmed notifiable disease with its extent and route

options.label: European foulbrood
options.detail: Melissococcus plutonius not detected

options.label: Sacbrood virus infection
options.detail: Larvae would be sac-like and not ropy, and the culture is positive for P. larvae

options.label: Varroosis with secondary viral disease
options.detail: Low mite counts and the wrong brood lesions

options.label: Chalkbrood
options.detail: A fungal disease producing hard mummies, not ropy remains

stages.explanation: American foulbrood is notifiable in most jurisdictions, and naming it triggers a statutory process rather than a treatment plan: the bee inspector is informed, affected colonies and their frames are destroyed by burning, equipment is sterilised or destroyed, and the apiary is placed under a standstill. Recording the shared-equipment route is what changes the beekeeper’s practice afterwards.
